questiontext.text:
(a) The statement below is false. Find a counterexample: a value of \(n\) for which it fails.

Statement: {@stmtC@}

\(n =\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) The example above proved that if \(n\) is odd, then \(n^3 + 1\) is even. A student tries \(n = 2\) and finds \(2^3 + 1 = 9\), which is odd. What does this show?

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]
[[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
(a) A counterexample to ‘if A, then B’ is a value for which A is true and B is false. Here A is ‘\(n\) is {@hypword@}’. For example \(n = {@tce@}\) is {@hypword@}, and \({@fexpr@} = {@valce@}\), which is not prime. So the statement is false: test before you try to prove.

(b) The statement in the example says nothing about even numbers. \(n = 2\) makes the ‘then’ part false, but it does not make the ‘if’ part true, so it is not a counterexample. A value tests a statement only if it satisfies the statement’s conditions, as in the chapter on counterexamples.

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the second of the two statements proved on pp. 47-49 (if n is an odd integer then n³ + 1 is an even integer) in Section 9 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

node.description: A counterexample: hypothesis holds, conclusion fails

truefeedback.text: Yes. \(n = {@ans1@}\) is {@hypword@}, and \({@fexpr@} = {@val@}\), which is not prime[[if test='is(sf > 1)']] (it is divisible by {@sf@})[[/if]][[if test='is(val = 1)']] (1 is not a prime number)[[/if]]. One counterexample shows that the statement is false, so there is nothing to prove.

node.description: Diagnostic: the value does not satisfy the hypothesis

truefeedback.text: \(n = {@ans1@}\) is not {@hypword@}. A counterexample must make the ‘if’ part true and the ‘then’ part false.

falsefeedback.text: When \(n = {@ans1@}\), \({@fexpr@} = {@val@}\), which is prime, so this value agrees with the statement. Keep testing values of \(n\) that are {@hypword@}.

node.description: Nothing: 2 does not satisfy the hypothesis

truefeedback.text: Yes. The statement only makes a claim about odd \(n\), and 2 is not odd, so \(n = 2\) cannot test it. To test it, use odd values of \(n\).

node.description: Diagnostic: n = 2 taken as a counterexample

truefeedback.text: A counterexample must make the ‘if’ part of the statement true, as well as the ‘then’ part false. Check the ‘if’ part for \(n = 2\).
The converse is in fact true (\(n^3 + 1\) is even exactly when \(n\) is odd). And \(n = 2\) could not be a counterexample to it: that would need \(n^3 + 1\) to be even, and 9 is not.

falsefeedback.text: The example proved that \(n^3 + 1\) is even for every odd \(n\), so no odd number can fail. Which numbers does this option talk about, and is 2 one of them?

qtest.description: Value outside the hypothesis; n = 2 as counterexample
